course: 1C:Enterprise 8 Programming — from foundations to professional development
module: Platform architecture, infobases and development environments
title: How 1C works: platform, service design and your data
goal: Distinguish platform, configuration and infobase using your own service desk.

prerequisites.text: Open an application and create a separate directory. No prior applied-course completion is required.

sections.title: Three different things in one application
paragraphs: A service desk stores customers and repair requests. The 1C platform is installed software that displays windows, stores records and executes instructions. A configuration describes a particular application: its catalogs, fields, documents and actions. An infobase contains the application definition in use and its stored information. A notebook analogy helps initially: page structure resembles the definition and filled rows resemble data. A real infobase additionally maintains relationships, states and execution rules.

Renaming a customer changes one record; adding a document type changes the application definition. Two infobases can use identical configurations and contain different customers. Matching window titles therefore do not identify a working copy. Check the selected startup entry and its directory.

sections.title: One customer, two different changes
paragraphs: Window color and file extension do not determine the task.

Add a Services catalog → edit the configuration.

sections.title: Using the application or developing it
paragraphs: Enterprise mode is where users create and read records through application windows. Designer changes the definition and code. An empty infobase can have no Customers command because the catalog has not been defined. A missing command does not automatically mean the platform is broken.

We need no third-party accounting configuration. Exercises use our own service desk and invented data. First identify the right infobase; then create a small action with a visible result. The Start from zero link supplies official training-edition setup instructions before the first required launch.

sections.title: Program, instruction and module
paragraphs: A program describes actions in a particular order. An instruction is an individual action such as displaying a message. BSL is a common label for the 1C scripting language; .bsl identifies a module source-text file. A module belongs to a particular part of an application. A text file alone does not automatically create catalogs and forms.

Our first code lesson opens the managed application module in Designer and displays a message when the learner’s infobase starts. Saving source and executing it are different operations: update the database configuration and start the application after making changes. Exact buttons are explained before the first code task.

sections.title: Two similarly named infobases
paragraphs: The configuration name shown in a title can be identical in both copies.

code.output: Choose the intended startup entry and location.

sections.title: Where execution really happens
paragraphs: Interactive Nexus diagrams explain relationships; switching them does not execute BSL. Studio syntax highlighting does not run it either. Install the official training platform normally on your computer for native practice. Obtain its distribution from the rights holder; the course transfers no licenses and requires no paid service for the beginner route.

The training edition supports our small file infobase but has limitations. It cannot establish server-cluster behavior, concurrent users or professional access protection. OneScript is a separate environment with a similar language, not an automatic replacement for the platform. Identify the environment and action actually observed.

sections.title: Check your explanation
paragraphs: I think the Nexus page executes 1C. The page explains; BSL executes in the specified 1C environment.
I expect customer records in an empty configuration. Define the application object or use the prepared original training configuration first.
